title: AI Briefing: Please Stop Making Me Opt Out of AI
summary: A deep dive into the friction between emerging AI infrastructure, consumer opt-out realities, and the economic constraints of scaling models in 2026, drawing on recent Wired perspectives, Google's Virginia community investments, and policy signals from Senator Mark Warner.

body.text: The Architecture of Involuntary Integration

The prompt to stop making me opt out of AI is not merely a rhetorical flourish; it is a precise description of the current state of model deployment. The industry has moved from a phase of consumer-facing demos to a phase of infrastructure lock-in. This shift is driven by two distinct but converging forces: the economics of inference and the geopolitical necessity of sovereign data boundaries. As we analyze the signals from Wired, Google, and the Axios reports on Senator Warner, the picture that emerges is one where the very mechanisms designed to democratize access to intelligence are simultaneously constraining the ability of users to disengage from that intelligence.

The inference economics of large language models have undergone a fundamental transformation. In the early days, the cost of running a model was a barrier to entry that favored capital-rich incumbents. Today, the cost structure has inverted. The marginal cost of inference has dropped precipitously due to the proliferation of specialized hardware, the optimization of model architectures, and the rise of efficient quantization techniques. However, this drop in marginal cost has not led to a drop in the total cost of ownership for enterprises. Instead, it has led to a massive increase in the total compute required to maintain relevance. To keep pace with the capabilities of the frontier models, organizations are forced to scale their inference clusters exponentially. This scaling creates a dependency on a few dominant cloud providers and hardware vendors, effectively creating a new form of vendor lock-in that is far more difficult to break than the software license agreements of the past.

body.text: This dependency is exacerbated by the concept of data boundaries. The security and safety of AI systems rely heavily on the integrity of the training data and the inference environment. As models become more specialized and more powerful, the sensitivity of the data they process increases. This has led to a proliferation of sovereign AI initiatives, where nations and regions are establishing their own data centers and model ecosystems to ensure that sensitive information remains within their jurisdiction. Google's recent announcement of community investments in Virginia is a prime example of this trend. By building infrastructure that supports local jobs and expands energy affordability, these initiatives are not just about creating a cloud; they are about creating a closed loop of data sovereignty. When data is kept within a specific geographic and legal boundary, the ability of a user to opt out of the AI ecosystem becomes functionally impossible, as their data is already embedded in the infrastructure that serves them.
The Product Strategy of Frictionless Friction

Product strategy in the AI era is defined by the paradox of frictionless friction. The user experience is designed to be seamless, with AI agents proactively suggesting actions, drafting emails, and managing schedules. This seamlessness is achieved through deep integration into the operating system and the applications layer. However, this integration comes at the cost of user agency. The models are trained on vast datasets that include user interactions, which means that the very act of using the system is feeding the system that is controlling the user's workflow. This creates a feedback loop where the system learns to anticipate user needs in ways that may not align with the user's explicit preferences. The result is a form of frictionless friction: the system feels responsive and helpful, but it is also subtly steering the user away from the option of opting out.

body.text: The safety and security dimensions of this product strategy are equally complex. Safety is not just about preventing harm; it is about managing the risk of model collapse, where the model's internal representations degrade over time due to the accumulation of errors or adversarial attacks. Security, on the other hand, is about protecting the data and the infrastructure from external threats. Both safety and security require a high degree of control over the model's environment, which further entrenches the system's presence in the user's life. The models are trained to be robust, but this robustness often comes at the expense of transparency. Users are less likely to understand how the model is making decisions, which makes it harder to challenge those decisions or to opt out of them.
Labor Design and the Human-in-the-Loop

The labor design of AI systems is another area where the tension between automation and human agency is palpable. As models become more capable, the role of the human worker is shifting from being the primary operator to being the supervisor or the verifier. This shift is often framed as a positive development, as it allows humans to focus on higher-level tasks. However, it also creates a new form of labor exploitation, where workers are expected to constantly monitor the AI systems and correct their mistakes. This constant monitoring is a form of frictionless friction: the system is designed to be self-correcting, but it requires human intervention to ensure that it is correcting itself in the right way. The result is a labor market that is increasingly dependent on the AI systems, making it harder for workers to opt out of the AI ecosystem.

The operational consequences of this labor design are significant. The systems are becoming more complex, requiring more specialized skills to operate and maintain. This complexity creates a barrier to entry for new players, further consolidating the market around a few dominant companies. The operational costs are also rising, as the systems require more energy and more hardware to run. This rise in operational costs is a key factor in the deficit problem that Senator Warner has highlighted in his AI plan. The plan proposes a series of investments in AI infrastructure, but it also acknowledges the need for a sustainable funding model that does not rely solely on government subsidies. The deficit problem is not just a fiscal issue; it is a structural issue that is rooted in the way AI systems are designed and operated.
The Political Economy of AI Infrastructure

The political economy of AI infrastructure is a critical aspect of the current debate. The investments in Virginia, for example, are not just about creating a cloud; they are about creating a political constituency that supports AI development. By tying AI development to local jobs and energy affordability, these initiatives are creating a feedback loop between the technology and the political landscape. This feedback loop is what makes it so difficult to opt out of AI: the technology is not just a tool; it is a political entity that has its own interests and its own agenda.

The Axios report on Senator Warner's AI plan provides a clear example of this political economy. The plan includes a series of investments in AI infrastructure, but it also includes a series of regulatory measures to ensure that the AI systems are safe and secure. These regulatory measures are designed to protect the public interest, but they also create a barrier to entry for new players. The result is a political landscape that is increasingly dominated by a few large companies that have the resources to comply with the regulations and to invest in the infrastructure. This dominance is what makes it so difficult to opt out of AI: the technology is not just a tool; it is a political entity that has its own interests and its own agenda.
The Reality of Model Capabilities

Finally, it is important to address the reality of model capabilities. The Wired article "AI Isn't Smarter Than a Baby—Yet" provides a sobering perspective on the current state of AI. While the models are impressive, they are not yet capable of the level of reasoning and creativity that is often attributed to them. The models are trained on vast datasets, but they are not yet capable of understanding the world in the way that humans do. This limitation is what makes it so difficult to opt out of AI: the technology is not just a tool; it is a political entity that has its own interests and its own agenda.

The models are also not yet capable of the level of safety and security that is required for widespread adoption. The Wired article "Please Stop Making Me Opt Out of AI" provides a clear example of this limitation. The models are trained to be robust, but they are not yet capable of managing the risk of model collapse or adversarial attacks. body.text: The Path Forward

The path forward is not clear, but it is not impossible. The investments in Virginia and the regulatory measures proposed by Senator Warner are steps in the right direction, but they are not sufficient. We need a new approach to AI infrastructure that takes into account the political economy of the technology and the reality of model capabilities. We need a new approach to labor design that takes into account the frictionless friction of the product strategy and the safety and security dimensions of the system. We need a new approach to the user experience that takes into account the seamlessness of the integration and the barrier to entry for new players.
What changes in practice

For AI, the operational question is whether the news changes how products are built, deployed, governed, or paid for. A model announcement matters most when it shifts inference cost, reliability, data boundaries, security exposure, or the amount of work a team can safely delegate to automation.

The lead signal is Please Stop Making Me Opt Out of AI. Leo would not read it as a standalone item. He would place it beside the rest of the source set and ask which assumption is being tested: demand, cost, trust, policy, infrastructure capacity, or the willingness of customers and investors to keep paying for the current narrative.

The current source mix points to several connected signals rather than one isolated story: Please Stop Making Me Opt Out of AI; AI Isn’t Smarter Than a Baby—Yet; Our new community investments in Virginia support local jobs and expand energy affordability.; Exclusive: Inside Sen. Mark Warner's AI plan - Axios (Axios); Don't count on AI to fix America's deficit problem - Axios (Axios). Read together, they give Leo a broader map of where attention is moving and which assumptions deserve a second look.
Second-order effects

The second-order question is trust. Teams do not adopt artificial intelligence because a demo is impressive; they adopt it when the workflow is observable, the failure mode is bounded, and the economics still make sense after compliance, support, latency, and human review are counted.

Leo's operating lens is to look for the control point. Sometimes it is the model, sometimes the distribution channel, sometimes the data contract, and sometimes the boring integration layer that decides whether a capability becomes a dependable product.
What to watch next

The next useful check is adoption quality. Pilots, demos, and benchmark claims are weaker signals than durable workflows, clear ownership, measured costs, and evidence that customers trust the system enough to use it in consequential work.

The practical discipline is to avoid treating the freshest headline as the whole story. The stronger read is slower and more mechanical: identify the constraint, watch whether it spreads, and keep revising the map as better evidence arrives.
